the diversity of bacterial species in blood samples from neutropenic patients is higher than previously recognized, and that this diversity is mainly composed of opportunistic human pathogens, with the largest proportion of bacteria belonging to the Proteobacteria phylum.
high throughput sequencing is able to detect a much broader diversity and quantity of bacteria than culture in neutropenic patients with BSI.
the diversity of bacteria detected in neutropenia is much higher than previously recognized.

the bacterial landscape in blood samples from neutropenic patients with fever.
the development of new approaches for the diagnosis of BSI, which could lead to a more targeted use of antibiotics.
the identification of bacteria in BSI by high throughput sequencing and the characterization of the bacterial diversity in this disease.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the microbiota of neutropenic patients is not only a reservoir for opportunistic bacteria but also for a wide variety of other microorganisms, which may play a significant role in the pathophysiology of the neutropenic state.
the bacterial landscape in neutropenic patients is more diverse than previously thought, and that the bacterial diversity is likely to be of host origin.
the microbiota of neutropenic patients is not sterile but contains a broad diversity of bacteria, which are mostly opportunistic human pathogens.

high throughput sequencing is a useful tool to detect bacterial pathogens in neutropenic patients.
the microbiome in BSI is much more diverse than the microbiome in the gut and that this diversity is likely host derived.
the bacterial diversity of BSI is much higher than expected.

the current culture-based methods used to diagnose BSI may be insufficient to provide a full picture of the bacterial diversity present in these infections.
blood culture is not a reliable method of identifying the causative agent of BSI in neutropenic patients.
the microbiome is a dynamic entity that can be altered by the host and the environment.
